title: The Mentoring Prison Officer
author: Unlocked Graduates
summary: This post from Unlocked Graduates describes the Mentoring Prison Officer role, a two-year secondment in which experienced officers coach new graduate recruits through their first two years on the landings. It sets out the weekly rhythm of observation, fortnightly coaching, group supervision and ongoing training, backed by detailed reporting. The authors argue the model works because mentors are selected rigorously on values and responsibility, placed outside the prisons where participants work, trained in instructional coaching themselves, and held accountable for retention. They report that Unlocked officers are 18 percentage points more likely to be in post after two years than standard-route entrants. The piece is candid about failure modes, including mentors seeking an easy escape from operations, reliance on anecdote, and drift into wellbeing support at the expense of practice development. It closes by arguing the lessons should be built into the middle-manager rank so that every new officer receives this level of support.
points: Selecting mentors on mission, values and a high sense of responsibility for every outcome matters more than skill, because skills can be trained and values far less so.
Placing mentors outside the home establishment buys trust, availability and an independent voice that insiders cannot offer.
Coaching is a skill in its own right, so mentors themselves need a structured training programme and a weekly day of development.
Support that slides into wellbeing alone was associated with weaker performance and retention, so mentoring has to stay anchored in structured practice development.
The long-term goal is to move the mentoring habit into the line-manager role so that development does not depend on a seconded few.
quotes: Being a prison officer is hard, so officers need ongoing training and support, and they need the most of it in their first year or two. Unlocked’s Mentoring Prison Officers (MPOs) provide it. They support Unlocked participants, the graduates on our two-year programme, through their first two years on the landings.

Mission and values come first. All skills are trainable; values much less so. We look for the ability to take responsibility, belief that prisoners can rehabilitate, and respect for the prison officer role.

MPOs are explicitly not placed in their home establishment. They bring the domain knowledge to help participants grow as officers, but they don’t carry the risk that sensitive information gets passed on.

Supporting new officers to develop expertise is a complex skill, so MPOs complete a structured training programme of their own, which teaches them to support staff to be effective and stay in the role. It begins with a four-week induction.

The most recent MoJ data shows Unlocked officers are 18 percentage points more likely to be in post after two years than officers entering through the standard route. That is despite close to nine in ten of our participants not having considered a career in the prison service before hearing about Unlocked, and many being actively pursued by other employers during the programme.

Drifting into wellbeing support. In Unlocked’s early days, before we had codified strategies, MPO support often slid into wellbeing support. Our data shows that participants whose MPOs focused on wellbeing rather than structured practice development were associated with lower performance, less enjoyment of the job and poorer retention, both on the programme and in prison afterwards.

Escaping operations. The biggest risk is people applying to be mentors to escape being an operational officer, either because they don’t enjoy the role or because they want an easy life. We have found that having the wrong people mentoring new staff is the single biggest risk to the model failing.

The MPO model works because it puts the right people, with real prestige and proper training, outside the pressures of the establishment. But a seconded mentor is not a permanent answer for every new officer.
